 Follow Us On: News Business Personal Finance 8th Pay Commission: 1 year later, 3 big questions employees want answered 8th Pay Commission: 1 year later, 3 big questions employees want answered
 A year has passed since the 8th Pay Commission was set up, but several key questions remain unanswered. From the salary hike to the fitment factor, here's what central government employees are waiting to know.
 Advertisement The 8th Pay Commission has completed a year, but the big salary questions remain. By: India Today Business Desk New Delhi , Nov 4, 2026 11:58 IST Last Updated Nov 4, 2026 11:58 IST Published by Jasmine anand Nov 4, 2026 11:58 IST Written By Jasmine Anand A year has passed since the 8th Pay Commission was formally set up, but central government employees are still waiting for answers on some important questions. How much will their salaries increase? What will the fitment factor be? And when can they expect the revised pay structure to come into effect?
 Formally established on November 3, 2025, the 8th Central Pay Commission is tasked with reviewing the salaries, allowances and pensions of central government employees and pensioners. Its recommendations are expected to benefit more than 50 lakh employees and nearly 69 lakh pensioners.
 advertisement ❮ ❯ Read Full Story While the commission has begun its preparatory work, crucial details such as the final fitment factor, the extent of the salary hike and the implementation timeline are still awaited. Here are three big questions employees want answered. HOW MUCH WILL SALARIES RISE UNDER THE 8TH PAY COMMISSION ?
 One of the biggest expectations surrounding the 8th Pay Commission is an increase in basic salaries. To understand how significant the next revision could be, it is worth looking at how government pay has changed over the years.
 Minimum basic pay for central government employees has increased from Rs 55 under the First Pay Commission to Rs 18,000 under the Seventh Pay Commission. The salary structure has also evolved over time.
 Under the Seventh Pay Commission, the earlier Pay Band and Grade Pay system was replaced with a Pay Matrix, bringing a more structured approach to salary levels and increments.
 Explaining this evolution, Adhil Shetty, CEO of Bankbazaar, said, "The evolution of government pay since independence shows how significantly the structure and level of basic pay have changed over time. Minimum basic pay for central government employees has risen from Rs 55 under the 1st Pay Commission to Rs 18,000 under the 7th Pay Commission."
 He added that the Pay Matrix had replaced the earlier Pay Band and Grade Pay system under the Seventh Pay Commission, and the Eighth Pay Commission would determine the next revision to this structure.
 However, the actual increase in basic salaries will depend on the recommendations made by the commission and the government's final decision. WHAT WILL THE FITMENT FACTOR BE?
 If there is one number that employees are particularly keen to know, it is the fitment factor. This multiplier will play a major role in determining the revised basic pay of employees and pensions of retirees.
 In simple terms, the fitment factor is applied to the existing basic salary or pension to arrive at the revised amount. A higher multiplier would mean a bigger increase in basic pay, while a lower one would result in a more modest revision.
 For instance, an employee currently drawing a basic salary of Rs 18,000 would see the revised amount calculated by multiplying the existing basic pay by the fitment factor eventually recommended and approved.
 advertisement Even a small difference in the multiplier can make a significant difference to monthly earnings, particularly across different pay levels.
 This explains why employees and pensioners are closely following discussions about the possible fitment factor. However, no final figure has been announced yet, and estimates doing the rounds should not be treated as confirmed numbers. WHEN WILL THE REVISED SALARIES COME INTO EFFECT?
 The third big question is about the timeline. Employees want to know when the commission will submit its recommendations, when the government will approve them and when the revised salaries will actually reflect in their pay slips.
 The commission has started some of its preparatory work. In April 2026, it invited applications for engaging consultants to assist with its assignments.
 According to the notification, consultants would be hired for fixed periods to provide specialised services and handle specific, time-bound assignments. They would not be engaged for routine day-to-day work. The engagement could be on a full-time or part-time basis.
 Their responsibilities include analysing salaries, pay structures, allowances and pensions across different employee categories, reviewing existing emoluments, and studying reports, databases and surveys to identify trends in compensation and demographics.
 advertisement Consultants may also assist with legal research, coordinate with government ministries and departments to collect information, examine representations submitted to the commission and assess the financial impact of proposed changes.
 The work will also cover specialised studies on human resource and compensation issues, including a review of gratuity and bonus mechanisms.
 These activities indicate that the commission is gathering the information needed to assess the existing pay structure and work towards its recommendations. However, the exact timeline for submitting the report and implementing the revised salaries remains unclear.
 For now, central government employees and pensioners will have to wait for clarity on these three crucial aspects. The fitment factor, the extent of the salary hike and the implementation date will ultimately determine how much the 8th Pay Commission changes their monthly earnings and retirement benefits. - Ends
